requirements.requirement: On node1, serve the inventory application over TCP port 8181 while mandatory access control is enforcing.
requirements.summary: Direct checks show the inventory application listening on 0.0.0.0:8181, returning healthy and inventory responses, with AppArmor enabled and its process confined by the inventory-server profile in enforce mode. The same state was observed after a reboot.

overall_summary: The task outcome is satisfied. The inventory service is directly demonstrated on TCP 8181 under an enforcing AppArmor profile. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete: it records a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service, application data, listener, and MAC state. The fixed post-executor boot identity corroborates the reported new boot.
limitations: The lifecycle collector does not independently probe AppArmor state or application responses; those observations come from executor commands, though they are direct and coherent.
The lifecycle failed-service probe is unsupported on this OpenRC-based Alpine node, so it cannot independently rule out unrelated failed services.
Lifecycle snapshots provide only bounded temporary-file, socket, package-health, and platform observations rather than a comprehensive filesystem/configuration diff.

operational_hygiene.summary: The substantive mutations—installing AppArmor, creating the application and service, configuring its enforcing profile, and enabling persistent boot settings—were causally connected to the task. Minor retained residue reduced hygiene: an unused Python bytecode cache remained from syntax validation (cmd-c43066ed18e94452), the pre-AppArmor boot configuration backup was not removed after successful recovery verification (cmd-e5d34b65ad444278), and two temporary reboot log files remained (cmd-0d4cf8ea09634a26, cmd-6e2e20a0a7d34d07). These were bounded and low risk. Package-health output was unchanged from the pre-task snapshot.
